claim: Germ band extension is driven by active T1 processes that self-organize through positive feedback acting on tensions.
source: Our analysis provides evidence that germ band extension is driven by active T1 processes that self-organize through positive feedback acting on tensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of tension dynamics during T1 transitions, showing nonlinearly increasing tension on contracting interfaces (Figure 2D), and by the minimal model incorporating positive tension feedback (Figure 3).

claim: Epithelial convergent extension results from the controlled transformation of internal force balance geometry which combines the effects of bottom-up local self-organization with the top-down, embryo-scale regulation by gene expression.
source: More generally, our findings suggest that epithelial convergent extension results from the controlled transformation of internal force balance geometry which combines the effects of bottom-up local self-organization with the top-down, embryo-scale regulation by gene expression.
evidence: This claim synthesizes findings from the entire study, including the role of genetic patterning in setting initial conditions and mechanical properties, and the role of mechanical feedback in coordinating cell behaviors.

claim: The Drosophila embryo is one of the best-established models of developmental mechanics as it is ideal for live imaging and offers an extensive set of genetic tools.
source: The Drosophila embryo is one of the best-established models of developmental mechanics as it is ideal for live imaging and offers an extensive set of genetic tools (Hales et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hales et al., 2015, which provides evidence for the utility of Drosophila as a model system.

claim: During Drosophila gastrulation, the embryonic blastoderm undergoes dramatic deformation that changes tissue topology and gives rise to the three germ layers.
source: During Drosophila gastrulation, the embryonic blastoderm (an epithelial monolayer of about 6000 cells on the surface of the embryo) undergoes dramatic deformation that changes tissue topology and gives rise to the three germ layers (Gilbert and Barresi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gilbert and Barresi, 2016, a standard developmental biology textbook.

claim: Gastrulation starts with the formation of the ventral furrow which initiates the internalization of mesoderm, followed immediately by germ band extension.
source: Gastrulation starts (see Figure 1A) with the formation of the ventral furrow (VF) which initiates the internalization of mesoderm, followed immediately by germ band extension (GBE), which involves convergent extension of the lateral ectoderm (or germ band) and the flow of tissue from the ventral onto the dorsal side of the embryo (Leptin, 1995; Martin et al., 2009; Martin, 2020; see Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leptin, 1995; Martin et al., 2009; Martin, 2020, and by Figure 1A and Video 1 showing the sequence of events.

claim: Germ band extension involves convergent extension of the lateral ectoderm and the flow of tissue from the ventral onto the dorsal side of the embryo.
source: Gastrulation starts (see Figure 1A) with the formation of the ventral furrow (VF) which initiates the internalization of mesoderm, followed immediately by germ band extension (GBE), which involves convergent extension of the lateral ectoderm (or germ band) and the flow of tissue from the ventral onto the dorsal side of the embryo (Leptin, 1995; Martin et al., 2009; Martin, 2020; see Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by visual evidence in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Concomitant with GBE, the posterior midgut moves from the posterior pole towards the anterior on the dorsal side of the embryo and invaginates progressively as it moves.
source: Concomitant with GBE, the posterior midgut (PMG) moves from the posterior pole towards the anterior on the dorsal side of the embryo and invaginates progressively as it moves.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tissue deformation is the sum of cell shape changes and cell rearrangements.
source: Tissue deformation is the sum of cell shape changes (top) and cell rearrangements (bottom).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1B and is a fundamental concept in tissue tectonics analysis.

claim: The elementary cell rearrangement is a T1 transition in a quartet of cells where the interface between two cells collapses and a new interface forms between two other cells.
source: The elementary cell rearrangement is a T1 transition in a quartet of cells: The interface between the red cells collapses, giving rise to a transient fourfold vertex configuration (center); the fourfold vertex then resolves to form a new interface between the blue cells.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1B and is a well-established concept in the field.

claim: During VFI, the lateral ectoderm is stretched along the DV axis and slightly contracts along the AP axis.
source: During VFI, the lateral ectoderm is stretched along the DV axis and slightly contracts along the AP axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GBE has an initial fast phase before slowing down at around 40 min.
source: GBE has an initial fast phase before slowing down at around 40 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During VFI, there are few intercalations.
source: During VFI, there are few intercalations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: During GBE, a majority of intercalations are T1 transitions, while rosettes contribute significantly less to tissue deformation.
source: During GBE, a majority of intercalations are T1 transitions, while rosettes – rearrangements involving more than four cells – contribute significantly less to tissue deformation (E').
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E and E'.

claim: At 40 min, there is a noticeable drop in the T1 rate, marking the transition to the slow phase of GBE.
source: At 40 min, there is a noticeable drop in the T1 rate, marking the transition to the slow phase of GBE.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The prevalence of T1s is consistent with previous analyses.
source: This prevalence of T1s is consistent with previous analyses (Farrell et al., 2017; Stern et al., 2022) and with the high coordination of rearrangements that is apparent in the lateral ectoderm (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Farrell et al., 2017 and Stern et al., 2022.

claim: Intercalations are associated with localized activity of the force-generating protein non-muscle myosin II.
source: Intercalations are associated with localized activity of the force-generating protein non-muscle myosin II (Bertet et al., 2004; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Martin, 2020) (henceforth simply 'myosin').
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertet et al., 2004; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Martin, 2020.

claim: The relative contribution of locally generated forces vs pulling by adjacent tissues, such as the invaginating PMG remain debated.
source: However, the relative contribution of such locally generated forces vs pulling by adjacent tissues, such as the invaginating PMG remain debated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fact that previous studies have come to conflicting conclusions, as cited.

claim: Previous studies addressing the question of internal vs external forces on the tissue level have come to conflicting conclusions.
source: Previous studies addressing this key questions on the tissue level have come to conflicting conclusions (Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994; Streichan et al., 2018; Collinet et al., 2015; Butler et al., 2009; Lye et al., 2015; Farrell et al., 2017; Gehrels et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies with different conclusions.

claim: Myosin recruitment depends on the expression of key developmental genes.
source: Myosin recruitment depends on the expression of key developmental genes (Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Martin et al., 2009; Lecuit et al., 2011; Martin, 2020), and, in addition, is subject to positive and negative mechanical feedback that depends on the stress (Blankenship et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009) and the rate of strain (rate of cell deformation) (Gustafson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Myosin recruitment is subject to positive and negative mechanical feedback that depends on the stress and the rate of strain.
source: Myosin recruitment depends on the expression of key developmental genes (Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Martin et al., 2009; Lecuit et al., 2011; Martin, 2020), and, in addition, is subject to positive and negative mechanical feedback that depends on the stress (Blankenship et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009) and the rate of strain (rate of cell deformation) (Gustafson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blankenship et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Gustafson et al., 2022.

claim: The relative roles of the genetic pre-pattern (top-down) vs local 'self-organization' of myosin activity via mechanical feedback loops (bottom-up) are still unclear.
source: Despite considerable understanding of the genetic and cell-biological components involved in GBE, the relative roles of the genetic pre-pattern (top-down) vs local 'self-organization' of myosin activity via mechanical feedback loops (bottom-up) are still unclear.
evidence: This claim reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and motivates the study.

claim: Cortical force balance provides a direct link between mechanics and geometry.
source: Cortical force balance provides a direct link between mechanics and geometry: It allows inference of tensions from the angles at the vertices where interfaces meet (Chiou et al., 2012; Ishihara et al., 2013; Noll et al., 2020), which we utilize to identify from images the stereotyped local geometry and tension dynamics associated with internally driven (active) and externally driven (passive) cell rearrangements (T1s).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiou et al., 2012; Ishihara et al., 2013; Noll et al., 2020, which describe tension inference methods.

claim: Tension inference allows inference of tensions from the angles at the vertices where interfaces meet.
source: Cortical force balance provides a direct link between mechanics and geometry: It allows inference of tensions from the angles at the vertices where interfaces meet (Chiou et al., 2012; Ishihara et al., 2013; Noll et al., 2020), which we utilize to identify from images the stereotyped local geometry and tension dynamics associated with internally driven (active) and externally driven (passive) cell rearrangements (T1s).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that developed and validated tension inference methods.

claim: The capacity of epithelial tissue to support tension makes it markedly different from passive fluids.
source: The capacity of epithelial tissue to support tension makes it markedly different from passive fluids (Noll et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Noll et al., 2017.

claim: The morphogenetic flow of epithelia can be understood as adiabatic deformation of cell array geometry controlled by changes in the internal state of tension.
source: Our findings suggest that the morphogenetic flow of epithelia can be understood as adiabatic deformation of cell array geometry controlled by changes in the internal state of tension.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from the tension-isogonal decomposition and the minimal model presented in the study.

claim: The tissue behaves as a plastically deforming active solid rather than a fluid.
source: In other words, the tissue behaves as a plastically deforming active solid rather than a fluid.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the findings regarding force balance and tension dynamics.

claim: Coordination of active T1 events among neighboring cells involves a characteristic pattern of cortical tensions which is quantified by the 'local tension configuration (LTC)' order parameter.
source: We will show that coordination of active T1 events among neighboring cells involves a characteristic pattern of cortical tensions which we quantify by introducing the 'local tension configuration (LTC)' order parameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of local tension configurations presented in Figure 8.

claim: Mechanical stress in the epithelium is primarily carried by the adherens-junctional cytoskeleton, which resides on cell interfaces.
source: We further assume that mechanical stress in the epithelium is primarily carried by the adherens-junctional cytoskeleton, which resides on cell interfaces.
evidence: This assumption is supported by the observation that cell-cell interfaces in the Drosophila blastoderm are mostly straight.

claim: Cell-cell interfaces in the Drosophila blastoderm are mostly straight.
source: This is supported by the observation that cell-cell interfaces in the Drosophila blastoderm are mostly straight.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the imaging data.

claim: The Drosophila blastoderm lies on top of a fluid yolk which exerts negligible drag forces on tissue motion on the surface.
source: The Drosophila blastoderm lies on top of a fluid yolk (Doubrovinski et al., 2017) which exerts negligible drag forces on tissue motion on the surface (Cheikh et al., 2022), suggesting that all forces are balanced within the epithelial layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doubrovinski et al., 2017 and Cheikh et al., 2022.

claim: All forces are balanced within the epithelial layer.
source: The Drosophila blastoderm lies on top of a fluid yolk (Doubrovinski et al., 2017) which exerts negligible drag forces on tissue motion on the surface (Cheikh et al., 2022), suggesting that all forces are balanced within the epithelial layer.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that the yolk exerts negligible drag forces.

claim: In the lateral ectoderm, high-tension interfaces contract.
source: In the lateral ectoderm, high-tension interfaces contract.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C'.

claim: The regular pattern of alternating high and low tension interfaces leads to coordinated T1s.
source: The regular pattern of alternating high and low tension interfaces therefore leads to coordinated T1s (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C' and Figure 1C.

claim: Active and passive T1s show similar dynamics of the length of the inner edge.
source: While active and passive T1s show similar dynamics of the length of the inner edge (top), they are markedly different in their tension dynamics (bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Active and passive T1s are markedly different in their tension dynamics.
source: While active and passive T1s show similar dynamics of the length of the inner edge (top), they are markedly different in their tension dynamics (bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Increasing tension on contracting interfaces provides evidence for positive tension feedback in the lateral ectoderm.
source: Increasing tension on contracting interfaces provides evidence for positive tension feedback in the lateral ectoderm (D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Constant relative tension on contracting tensions in the dorsal ectoderm indicates passive intercalations.
source: Constant relative tension on contracting tensions in the dorsal ectoderm indicates passive intercalations (E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increasing tension on an actively contracting interface causes the angles opposite of it to become increasingly acute.
source: Increasing tension on an actively contracting interface causes the angles opposite of it to become increasingly acute.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2F and follows from the geometric relationship between tension and angles.

claim: Constant cortical tensions before the neighbor exchange are the hallmarks of passive T1s.
source: Constant cortical tensions (and thus vertex angles) before the neighbor exchange are the hallmarks of passive T1s.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2G and supported by the data in Figure 2E.

claim: In the lateral ectoderm, relative tension predicts the time until an interface collapses.
source: In the lateral ectoderm, relative tension predicts the time until an interface collapses (H) and high relative tension predicts which interfaces collapse (J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2H and J.

claim: High relative tension predicts which interfaces collapse in the lateral ectoderm.
source: In the lateral ectoderm, relative tension predicts the time until an interface collapses (H) and high relative tension predicts which interfaces collapse (J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The non-linearly increasing tension, concomitant with an accelerating rate of interface contraction, is evidence that positive tension feedback plays a role in myosin recruitment.
source: Notably, the non-linearly increasing tension, concomitant with an accelerating rate of interface contraction, is evidence that positive tension feedback plays a role in myosin recruitment (Blankenship et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Duda et al., 2019) and is in excellent agreement with predictions from a recent model where such feedback is a key ingredient (Sknepnek et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blankenship et al., 2006; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Duda et al., 2019; Sknepnek et al., 2023, and by the data in Figure 2D.

claim: There is no correlation between relative tension and the time until the interface collapses in the amnioserosa.
source: As a consequence of this tension homeostasis on collapsing interfaces, there is no correlation between relative tension and the time until the interface collapses in the amnioserosa (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: On an extending junction, tension carried by passive crosslinkers will add to the tension generated by myosin.
source: On an extending junction, tension carried by passive crosslinkers will add to the tension generated by myosin.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the mechanical properties of the cytoskeleton.

claim: The passive tension rapidly relaxes as crosslinkers turn over, giving an effective viscoelastic relaxation timescale on the order of minutes.
source: The passive tension rapidly relaxes as crosslinkers turn over, giving an effective viscoelastic relaxation timescale on the order of minutes (Clément et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clément et al., 2017.

claim: In the amnioserosa, the high tension is sustained for a longer time because the tissue there is continually getting stretched as the germ band contracts along the DV axis.
source: In the amnioserosa, the high tension is sustained for a longer time because the tissue there is continually getting stretched as the germ band contracts along the DV axis.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of sustained high tension in the amnioserosa and the understanding of the mechanical coupling between tissues.

claim: The length and tension of cell-cell interfaces can change independently and are actively regulated by the turnover of junctional proteins.
source: By contrast, the length and tension of cell-cell interfaces can change independently and are actively regulated by the turnover of junctional proteins (such as actin, myosin, and E-cadherin).
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the active regulation of the cytoskeleton.

claim: Experiments where actin turnover is decreased by Cytochalasin D treatment show reduced cell intercalations.
source: Experiments where actin turnover is decreased by Cytochalasin D treatment show reduced cell intercalations supporting the point of view that the decoupling of tension regulation from a spring-like constitutive relation is important for physiological behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental evidence, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: The minimal model directly builds on the same assumptions that underlie the tension inference: dominant cortical tensions that are in adiabatic force balance.
source: Instead, our model directly builds on the same assumptions that underlie the tension inference: dominant cortical tensions that are in adiabatic force balance.
evidence: This claim describes the basis of the minimal model presented in the study.

claim: The dynamics in the minimal model reside in the changes in tension governed by mechanical feedback.
source: The dynamics reside in the changes in tension governed by mechanical feedback.
evidence: This claim describes the key feature of the minimal model.

claim: The minimal model reproduces the signatures of active and passive T1s observed in the Drosophila embryo.
source: The model reproduces the signatures of active and passive T1s observed in the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of model results (Figure 3E, F) with experimental data (Figure 2D, E).

claim: Positive feedback drives the relative tension on the quartet's central interface towards the tension threshold.
source: Positive feedback drives the relative tension on the quartet's central interface towards the tension threshold discussed below (see Figure 4E) and thus drives active T1s.
evidence: This claim is based on the dynamics of the minimal model and is illustrated in Figure 4E.

claim: The myosin 'handover' model predicts that the myosin level on the newly formed interface is always lower than that on the collapsing interface.
source: Importantly, this 'handover' model predicts that the myosin level (not the total tension) on the newly formed interface is always lower than that on the collapsing interface, in agreement with experimental observations (Bertet et al., 2004; Rauzi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertet et al., 2004 and Rauzi et al., 2008.

claim: The model finds good qualitative agreement between the single-quartet model and experimental data for the tension dynamics.
source: Simulating this model, we find good qualitative agreement between the single-quartet model and experimental data, both for the tension dynamics (compare Figure 3E and F and Figure 2D and E) and for the tension–isogonal decomposition which we will introduce below (compare Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, A' and Figure 4C and C').
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of model results with experimental data in the cited figures.

claim: In the absence of positive tension feedback, the model successfully describes passive intercalations when the displacements of cell centroids are prescribed to mimic external stresses.
source: In the absence of positive tension feedback, the model successfully describes passive intercalations when the displacements of cell centroids are prescribed to mimic external stresses (Figure 3F; see Appendix 5 for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In the minimal model, no additional active mechanism is necessary for interface extension.
source: Notably, in our model, there is no additional active mechanism for interface extension.
evidence: This claim describes a key feature of the minimal model.

claim: Interface extension is a consequence of the fundamental temporal asymmetry of T1 processes: high myosin levels on the collapsing interface versus low myosin levels on the emerging interface.
source: Instead, interface extension is a consequence of the fundamental temporal asymmetry of T1 processes: high myosin levels on the collapsing interface versus low myosin levels on the emerging interface.
evidence: This claim is based on the logic of the minimal model.

claim: Dominant cortical tensions constrain the angles at vertices.
source: Dominant cortical tensions constrain the angles at vertices.
evidence: This claim is based on the principle of force balance.

claim: Interface lengths can change collectively while keeping those angles fixed via isogonal modes.
source: Interface lengths can change collectively while keeping those angles fixed via isogonal modes (Noll et al., 2017), as illustrated in Figure 4A.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Noll et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Isogonal modes represent cell and tissue deformations that take place under constant cortical tensions.
source: These isogonal modes, therefore, represent cell and tissue deformations that take place under constant cortical tensions.
evidence: This claim follows from the definition of isogonal modes.

claim: Isogonal deformations can be caused by external forces and cell-internal elasticity.
source: They can be caused, for instance, by external forces and cell-internal elasticity (medial myosin, stiffness of the nucleus, intermediate filaments).
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the mechanical forces acting on cells.

claim: The tension–isogonal decomposition decomposes cell and tissue deformations into deformations of the tension triangulation reflecting changing cortical tensions, and isogonal deformations reflecting all other mechanical forces.
source: These above considerations suggest that we can use the observed geometry of the cell array to decompose cell and tissue deformations into two distinct components: (i) deformations of the tension triangulation reflecting changing cortical tensions, and (ii) isogonal deformations reflecting all other mechanical forces.
evidence: This claim describes the tension–isogonal decomposition method developed in the study.

claim: The tension–isogonal decomposition only assumes the dominance of cortical tensions over other stresses in the tissue.
source: This decomposition only assumes the dominance of cortical tensions over other stresses in the tissue and in particular is independent of the specific form of the cell elastic energy Equation 2 we used in the minimal model above.
evidence: This claim describes the assumptions underlying the tension–isogonal decomposition.

claim: In the lateral ectoderm, tension-triangle deformation accounts for quartet shape deformation, indicating that tension dynamics drives the intercalation.
source: In the lateral ectoderm, tension-triangle deformation accounts for quartet shape deformation, indicating that tension dynamics drives the intercalation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The isogonal strain is approximately constant in the lateral ectoderm and slightly counteracts the deformation.
source: The isogonal strain is approximately constant and, in fact, slightly counteracts the deformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The slight counteraction of deformation by isogonal strain is a consequence of the ventral furrow invagination which pulls on the lateral ectoderm cells and passively stretches them along the DV axis.
source: This is a consequence of the ventral furrow invagination which pulls on the lateral ectoderm cells and passively stretches them along the DV axis.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the mechanical coupling between tissues.

claim: In the passively deforming amnioserosa, the tension mode is constant—indicating tension homeostasis—while the cell quartet deformation is entirely stored in the isogonal mode.
source: A very different picture emerges in the passively deforming amnioserosa (Figure 4C'). Here, the tension mode is constant—indicating tension homeostasis—while the cell quartet deformation is entirely stored in the isogonal mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C'.

claim: The tension–isogonal decomposition quantitatively distinguishes between active and passive intercalations.
source: Taken together, the tension–isogonal decomposition quantitatively distinguishes between active and passive intercalations.
evidence: This claim summarizes the utility of the tension–isogonal decomposition method.

claim: Tensions are controlled locally, while the isogonal modes accommodate external, non-local forces.
source: Tensions are controlled locally, while the isogonal modes accommodate external, non-local forces, such as pulling by adjacent tissue.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the tension–isogonal decomposition.

claim: Isogonal deformations are associated with passive deformations because active stresses in the lateral ectoderm are generated at interfaces.
source: We associate isogonal deformations with passive deformations because active stresses in the lateral ectoderm are generated at interfaces.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of where active stresses are generated in the tissue.

claim: In systems where active stresses are generated in the cell's interior, the isogonal mode is actively controlled.
source: In systems where active stresses are generated in the cell's interior, e.g., due to nuclear migration (Bocanegra-Moreno et al., 2023) or due to intracellular actin cables (Priess and Hirsh, 1986), the isogonal mode is actively controlled.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bocanegra-Moreno et al., 2023 and Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: Apical constriction during VF invagination is driven by medial myosin pulses that drive isogonal cell contractions.
source: Another example of this is apical constriction during VF invagination which is driven by medial myosin pulses that drive isogonal cell contractions (Noll et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Noll et al., 2017.

claim: The interface collapse can be driven by the isogonal mode, by changes in tensions, or by a mixture of both.
source: It is immediately apparent that the interface collapse can be driven by the isogonal mode, by changes in tensions, or by a mixture of both.
evidence: This claim follows from the T1 threshold diagram in Figure 4E.

claim: The corresponding isogonal deformation for passive T1s has an aspect ratio of 3, in good agreement with observations.
source: By a geometric construction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) one finds that the corresponding isogonal deformation has an aspect ratio of 3, in good agreement with observations (Figure 4C').
evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric construction and the data in Figure 4C'.

claim: In the case of isosceles triangles, sharing the same circumcircle implies that they form a square such that the critical relative tension can be read off from the length of the diagonal.
source: In the case of isosceles triangles, this implies that they form a square such that we can read off the critical relative tension from the length of the diagonal.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4D' and is based on geometric reasoning.

claim: The T1 threshold diagram quantifies how active and passive forces interact to drive cell intercalations.
source: This diagram quantifies how active and passive forces interact to drive cell intercalations.
evidence: This claim describes the utility of the T1 threshold diagram.

claim: Active tension dynamics and passive isogonal strain appear as orthogonal ways to drive T1s.
source: Active tension dynamics and passive isogonal strain appear as orthogonal ways to drive T1s, as illustrated by the red and blue arrows.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4E.

claim: Tissue-scale tension anisotropy sets the orientation of the interfaces which will collapse, and hence, the direction of tissue flow.
source: If cortical tensions are regulated by positive feedback, the tissue-scale tension anisotropy sets the orientation of the interfaces which will collapse, and hence, the direction of tissue flow.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of how positive feedback amplifies initial anisotropy.

claim: Tissue-scale anisotropy of active tension is central to driving and orienting convergent extension flow.
source: Therefore, tissue-scale anisotropy of active tension is central to driving and orienting convergent extension flow (Rauzi et al., 2008; Etournay et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2015; Streichan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rauzi et al., 2008; Etournay et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2015; Streichan et al., 2018.

claim: The inferred tension anisotropy is consistent with previously published experimental observations.
source: The inferred tension anisotropy (Figure 5B) and its time course (Figure 5C) are consistent with previously published experimental observations: During VF invagination, DV-oriented interfaces in the lateral ectoderm are stretched causing myosin recruitment (Gustafson et al., 2022), increasing tension anisotropy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 5B and C and by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2022.

claim: Strong DV alignment of tension anisotropy in the trunk is found already before VF invagination.
source: Remarkably, we find strong DV alignment of tension anisotropy in the trunk already before VF invagination (Figure 5D, 0 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The strong DV alignment of tension anisotropy before VF invagination supports the hypothesis that tension anisotropy is set up in the initial condition.
source: This supports our hypothesis that tension anisotropy is set up in the initial condition.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of tension anisotropy before VF invagination.

claim: As GBE progresses, the DV alignment of tension anisotropy decreases.
source: As GBE progresses, the DV alignment of tension anisotropy decreases (Figure 5C and D, 37 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Numerical simulations reproduce the loss of global tension anisotropy and show that it is responsible for the slowdown of GBE after a twofold extension.
source: Numerical simulations presented in the companion paper (Claussen et al., 2024) reproduce this loss of global tension anisotropy and show that it is responsible for the slowdown of GBE after a twofold extension.
evidence: This claim is supported by results from the companion paper.

claim: The isogonal strain tensor can be calculated for each individual triplet of cells that meet at a vertex.
source: Specifically, we exploit the fact that the isogonal strain tensor can be calculated for each individual triplet of cells that meet at a vertex (see Figure 6A and Appendix 3 for details).
evidence: This claim describes the method for calculating tissue-scale isogonal strain.

claim: At the end of VF invagination (25 min), significant isogonal strain has built up adjacent to the VF indicating that the tissue there is passively stretched by the invaginating VF.
source: At the end of VF invagination (25 min), significant isogonal strain has built up adjacent to the VF indicating that the tissue there is passively stretched by the invaginating VF (see the purple shaded region in Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The lateral ectoderm further dorsal also accumulates some isogonal extension along the DV axis.
source: The lateral ectoderm further dorsal also accumulates some isogonal extension along the DV axis (green shaded region, see time traces in Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The predicted relative tension threshold is in excellent agreement with the value found by tension inference.
source: This value is in excellent agreement with the value found by tension inference (Figure 2D), thus validating the model for active T1s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of the predicted value with the observed value in Figure 2D.

claim: A snail mutant lacks a VF.
source: This mutant lacks a VF as illustrated in Figure 7A (Gheisari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gheisari et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Almost no isogonal strain is found in the lateral ectoderm of the snail mutant.
source: As expected, we find almost no isogonal strain in the lateral ectoderm of the snail mutant (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: During GBE, the isogonal strain near the ventral furrow relaxes back to nearly isotropic, suggesting that the passive deformation stored in the isogonal mode is elastic rather than plastic.
source: During GBE, the isogonal strain near the ventral furrow relaxes back to nearly isotropic, suggesting that the passive deformation stored in the isogonal mode is elastic rather than plastic (Figure 6B' and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B' and C.

claim: The actively contracting lateral ectoderm stretches the dorsal tissue (amnioserosa) along the DV axis.
source: At the same time, the actively contracting lateral ectoderm stretches the dorsal tissue (amnioserosa) along the DV axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B' and C.

claim: The passive deformation of the amnioserosa is consistent with the transition of cells from columnar to squamous and low myosin density in the amnioserosa.
source: This passive deformation of the amnioserosa is consistent with the transition of cells from columnar to squamous (Stern et al., 2022) and low myosin density in the amnioserosa (Streichan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stern et al., 2022 and Streichan et al., 2018.

claim: There is significant isogonal strain just anterior of the PMG, suggesting that the convergent extension tissue flow near the dorsal pole exerts a pulling force on the PMG.
source: There is also significant isogonal strain just anterior of the PMG (highlighted by the dashed outline in Figure 6B'), as well as on the lateral side of the PMG, suggesting that the convergent extension tissue flow near the dorsal pole (Streichan et al., 2018) exerts a pulling force on the PMG.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B' and by a citation to Streichan et al., 2018.

claim: The tissue on the dorsal pole is stretched along the DV axis by active convergent extension in the germ band and contracts along the AP axis to conserve total cell area, leading to an anterior-ward pulling force on the PMG.
source: In this picture, the tissue on the dorsal pole is stretched along the DV axis by active convergent extension in the germ band and contracts along the AP axis to conserve total cell area, leading to an anterior-ward pulling force on the PMG.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the isogonal strain data.

claim: Quantitative re-analysis of previously published cauterization experiments provides independent evidence of a pulling force on the PMG.
source: Quantitative re-analysis of previously published cauterization experiments (Collinet et al., 2015) provides independent evidence of such a pulling force (see Appendix 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the re-analysis of data from Collinet et al., 2015.

claim: Isogonal strain identifies regions where passive tissue deformation is caused by mechanical coupling across the tissue.
source: Taken together, isogonal strain identifies regions where passive tissue deformation is caused by mechanical coupling across the tissue.
evidence: This claim summarizes the utility of the isogonal strain analysis.

claim: The absence of isogonal strain along the AP axis in the germ band provides strong evidence that the main driver of GBE is internally generated stress, rather than an external pulling force from the PMG.
source: Importantly, the absence of isogonal strain along the AP axis in the germ band provides strong evidence that the main driver of GBE is internally generated stress, rather than an external pulling force from the PMG.
evidence: This claim is based on the isogonal strain analysis.

claim: Tension patterns do not appear globally with perfect regularity, but rather as local motifs that can be distinguished based on the tension configuration at individual vertices.
source: Tension patterns do not appear globally with perfect regularity, but rather as local motifs that can be distinguished based on the tension configuration at individual vertices.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of tension patterns in the data.

claim: The elementary motif of the alternating tension pattern is a 'tension bridge' where a high-tension interface is surrounded by low-tension interfaces, corresponding to an obtuse triangle.
source: The elementary motif of the alternating tension pattern is a 'tension bridge' where a high-tension interface is surrounded by low-tension interfaces (see Figure 8A, right), corresponding to an obtuse triangle (Figure 8B, top right).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 8A and B.

claim: An acute tension triangle corresponds to the local motif of a tension cable, where neighboring interfaces along the cable are under high tension while those transverse to the cable are under low tension.
source: In contrast, an acute tension triangle (Figure 8F, bottom right) corresponds to the local motif of a tension cable, where neighboring interfaces along the cable are under high tension while those transverse to the cable are under low tension (see Figure 8A, left).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The tension triangle shape can be used to define a LTC parameter.
source: We can, therefore, use the tension triangle shape to define a LTC parameter.
evidence: This claim describes the definition of the LTC order parameter.

claim: The T1 threshold is at a lower anisotropy magnitude for tension bridges than for tension cables, indicating that the former are more efficient at driving active intercalations.
source: This threshold is at a lower anisotropy magnitude for tension bridges than for tension cables, indicating that the former are more efficient at driving active intercalations.
evidence: This claim is based on the position of the T1 threshold in the LTC-parameter space shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The fraction of tension bridges increases before the onset of GBE.
source: Two-dimensional histograms of the LTC-parameter distribution in the lateral ectoderm show that the fraction tension of bridges increases before the onset of GBE (see Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The bridge fraction reaches its maximum around 25 min, just at the onset of GBE.
source: The bridge fraction reaches its maximum around 25 min, just at the onset of GBE (see Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The pattern of tensions on the (sub-)cellular scale is biologically relevant to choreographing parallel T1s.
source: This suggests that the pattern of tensions on the (sub-)cellular scale is biologically relevant to choreographing parallel T1s.
evidence: This claim is based on the correlation between LTC order and the onset of GBE.

claim: Tension configurations beyond the T1 threshold are strongly suppressed.
source: Therefore, tension configurations beyond the T1 threshold are strongly suppressed (hatched region in Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: As cell intercalations take place in the lateral ectoderm, the fraction of tension bridges decreases and the fraction of tension cables increases.
source: We observe that as cell intercalations take place in the lateral ectoderm, the fraction of tension bridges decreases and the fraction of tension cables increases (see Figure 8C, 50 min; and Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The distribution of tension triangle shapes appears to approach that of a random Delaunay triangulation.
source: In fact, the distribution of tension triangle shapes appears to approach that of a random Delaunay triangulation (see Figure 8—figure supplement 2), a completely disordered distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The triangle edge flips can be statistically understood as a random 'mixing' process that generically causes a loss of LTC order and global alignment of tension anisotropy.
source: This suggests that the triangle edge flips can be statistically understood as a random 'mixing' process that generically causes a loss of LTC order and global alignment of tension anisotropy.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that the tension triangle shape distribution approaches that of a random triangulation.

claim: In a snail mutant, the lack of DV-stretching of the lateral ectoderm implies that T1s occur at a reduced tension anisotropy compared to the wild type.
source: Recall that in a snail mutant, the lack of DV-stretching of the lateral ectoderm implies that T1s occur at a reduced tension anisotropy compared to the wild type.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the snail mutant shown in Figure 7.

claim: The shifted T1 threshold affects tension bridges more than tension cables.
source: Figure 8B shows that the shifted T1 threshold affects tension bridges more than tension cables.
evidence: This claim is based on the T1 threshold diagram in Figure 8B.

claim: Tension-bridge configurations undergo T1s more rapidly in a snail mutant and, therefore, contribute less to the overall distribution of local tension configurations.
source: As a result, we expect that tension-bridge configurations undergo T1s more rapidly in a snail mutant and, therefore, contribute less to the overall distribution of local tension configurations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the shifted T1 threshold.

claim: No increase in the fraction of tension bridges is observed in the snail mutant.
source: Indeed, no increase in the fraction of tension bridges is observed in this mutant (orange line in Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Tissue deformations are driven by the adiabatic transformation of the force-balance geometry.
source: Tissue deformations are driven by the adiabatic transformation of this force-balance geometry, allowing the epithelium to rearrange like a fluid while supporting internal tension like a solid.
evidence: This claim summarizes the key concept of the study.

claim: The epithelium can rearrange like a fluid while supporting internal tension like a solid.
source: Tissue deformations are driven by the adiabatic transformation of this force-balance geometry, allowing the epithelium to rearrange like a fluid while supporting internal tension like a solid.
evidence: This claim describes the behavior of the epithelium as understood from the study.

claim: The behavior of the epithelium can be thought of as a form of plasticity where the internal 'reference' structure of the material can be actively remodeled.
source: Alternatively, one can think of this behavior as a form of plasticity where the internal 'reference' structure of the material can be actively remodeled, resulting in spatial displacement of material points.
evidence: This claim provides an alternative interpretation of the epithelial behavior.

claim: The focus on the force balance geometry associated with the internal structure is more useful as it holds the key to understanding possible mechanisms of active control.
source: However, the focus on the force balance geometry associated with the internal structure is more useful as it holds the key to understanding possible mechanisms of active control.
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for the approach taken in the study.

claim: Tension inference has been validated extensively in previous literature.
source: Importantly, tension–isogonal decomposition is based on the same assumptions as tension inference which has been validated extensively in previous literature (Ishihara et al., 2013; Kong et al., 2019; Noll et al., 2020; Cheikh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple validation studies.

claim: In the early Drosophila embryo, both active and passive cell rearrangements (T1 events) are observed.
source: In the early Drosophila embryo, we observe both active and passive cell rearrangements (T1 events).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of T1 events in different tissue regions.

claim: Both tension-driven and isogonal modes interact and contribute to tissue deformations at the same time.
source: Generally, both modes – tension-driven and isogonal – interact and contribute to tissue deformations at the same time.
evidence: This claim is based on the tension–isogonal decomposition analysis.

claim: Ventral furrow invagination isogonally stretches the lateral ectoderm which increases the tension threshold for active T1s there.
source: We have found that ventral furrow invagination isogonally stretches the lateral ectoderm which increases the tension threshold for active T1s there.
evidence: This claim is based on the isogonal strain analysis and the T1 threshold diagram.

claim: Analysis of a snail mutant embryo confirmed the prediction that the local relative tension threshold will be lower in mutants that lack a ventral furrow.
source: Indeed, analysis of a snail mutant embryo confirmed this prediction and thus validates that tension–isogonal decomposition captures the interplay of internal and external forces acting on a tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data from the snail mutant analysis.

claim: Experimental evidence shows that both internally generated stresses and external pulling by the posterior midgut contribute to germ band extension.
source: Experimental evidence shows that both processes contribute, making a nuanced, quantitative analysis necessary.
evidence: This claim is based on the review of previous experimental evidence.

claim: Previously published microscopy data from cauterization and mutant experiments were re-analyzed to quantify tissue flow.
source: We, therefore, re-analyzed microscopy data from previously published cauterization and mutant experiments (Collinet et al., 2015) to quantify tissue flow (see Appendix 6).
evidence: This claim describes the re-analysis performed in the study.

claim: The results from the quantitative analysis of cauterization experiments indicate that forces generated in the germ band contribute significantly to tissue flow.
source: The results from this quantitative analysis indicate that forces generated in the germ band contribute significantly to tissue flow.
evidence: This claim is based on the re-analysis of cauterization experiments.

claim: In mutants where posterior midgut invagination is disrupted, the germ band buckles forming ectopic folds or twists into a corkscrew shape as it extends.
source: In these mutants, the germ band buckles forming ectopic folds (Zusman and Wieschaus, 1985; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991) or twists into a corkscrew shape (Perkins et al., 1992; Smits et al., 2023) as it extends, pointing towards a buckling instability characteristic of internally driven extensile flows (Liu et al., 2006; Senoussi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zusman and Wieschaus, 1985; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991; Perkins et al., 1992; Smits et al., 2023.

claim: The buckling and twisting of the germ band in mutants points towards a buckling instability characteristic of internally driven extensile flows.
source: In these mutants, the germ band buckles forming ectopic folds (Zusman and Wieschaus, 1985; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991) or twists into a corkscrew shape (Perkins et al., 1992; Smits et al., 2023) as it extends, pointing towards a buckling instability characteristic of internally driven extensile flows (Liu et al., 2006; Senoussi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2006 and Senoussi et al., 2019.

claim: The main effect of PMG invagination on the germ band lies not in creating pulling forces, but rather in 'making room' to allow for its orderly extension.
source: This suggests that the main effect of PMG invagination on the germ band lies not in creating pulling forces, but rather in 'making room' to allow for its orderly extension.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the mutant phenotypes and the isogonal strain analysis.

claim: The tension–isogonal analysis yields a fine-grained picture with various regions of active and passive deformation.
source: To conclusively settle the debate, evidence from the cell scale – where the forces are generated – is needed. Such evidence is provided by our tension–isogonal analysis, which yields a fine-grained picture with various regions of active and passive deformation (see Figure 6B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B and B'.

claim: Tissue deformation in the germ band is driven by internal remodeling of tensions and, therefore, active.
source: It clearly shows that tissue deformation in the germ band is driven by internal remodeling of tensions and, therefore, active.
evidence: This claim is based on the tension–isogonal analysis.

claim: The amnioserosa, and the tissue just anterior and lateral of the invaginating posterior midgut deforms passively.
source: In stark contrast, the amnioserosa, and the tissue just anterior and lateral of the invaginating posterior midgut deforms passively.
evidence: This claim is based on the tension–isogonal analysis.

claim: Cells exert active stresses on each other and, at the same time, constantly sense their mechanical environment.
source: Cells exert active stresses on each other and, at the same time, constantly sense their mechanical environment (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Collinet and Lecuit, 2021; Pinheiro and Bellaïche, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Collinet and Lecuit, 2021; Pinheiro and Bellaïche, 2018.

claim: Mechanical stresses and strains can propagate over long distances and contain information about the tissue geometry.
source: Mechanical stresses and strains can propagate over long distances and contain information about the tissue geometry (e.g. in the form of hoop stresses Lefebvre et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2023.

claim: In an epithelium dominated by cortical tensions, the mechanical environment forms a 'tension space,' linked to physical space via force balance.
source: In an epithelium dominated by cortical tensions, this mechanical environment forms a 'tension space,' linked to physical space via force balance.
evidence: This claim describes the concept of tension space introduced in the study.

claim: Tension space takes the form of a triangulation which allows an intuitive visualization.
source: Tension space takes the form of a triangulation which allows an intuitive visualization.
evidence: This claim describes the geometric representation of tension space.

claim: The angles in the cell array are fixed by complementary angles in the tension triangulation.
source: The angles in the cell array are fixed by complementary angles in the tension triangulation.
evidence: This claim is based on the principle of force balance.

claim: The tensions are geometric dials cells can directly sense and control.
source: Thus, the tensions are geometric dials cells can directly sense and control.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of mechanosensing in cells.

claim: Cells can control their configuration in tension space by defining the local dynamics of cortical tension.
source: We found that cells can control their configuration in tension space by defining the local dynamics of cortical tension.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from the study.

claim: Two distinct behaviors were identified in experimental data: amplification of tension on the interfaces that are already most tense, and apparent tension homeostasis.
source: In experimental data from gastrulating Drosophila embryos, we identified two distinct behaviors: (i) amplification of tension on the interfaces that are already most tense, suggestive of positive tension feedback (observed in lateral ectoderm) and (ii) apparent tension homeostasis (observed in the amnioserosa).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of tension dynamics in different tissue regions.

claim: Mechanical homeostasis is found in various systems and organisms.
source: Mechanical homeostasis is found in various systems and organisms (Humphrey, 2008; Latorre et al., 2018; Stamenović and Smith, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Humphrey, 2008; Latorre et al., 2018; Stamenović and Smith, 2020.

claim: Tension homeostasis allows the amnioserosa to undergo large cell deformations while maintaining tissue integrity.
source: We hypothesize that tension homeostasis allows the amnioserosa to undergo large cell deformations while maintaining tissue integrity (Latorre et al., 2018; Jodoin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to Latorre et al., 2018 and Jodoin et al., 2015.

claim: Tension feedback continuously modifies local force balance, driving the change in cell and tissue geometry.
source: Tension feedback, on the other hand, continuously modifies local force balance, driving the change in cell and tissue geometry.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the role of tension feedback.

claim: To the extent that cortical responses can be controlled by spatially modulated gene expression, evolution has the means to define a program of non-trivial spatiotemporal dynamics of tissue during morphogenesis.
source: To the extent that cortical responses can be controlled by spatially modulated gene expression, evolution thus has the means to define a program of non-trivial spatiotemporal dynamics of tissue during morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the interplay between genetic control and mechanical feedback.

claim: Evidence for positive feedback is provided by the nonlinearly increasing inferred tension on contracting interfaces and by laser ablation experiments in earlier work.
source: Evidence for positive feedback is provided by the nonlinearly increasing inferred tension on contracting interfaces (Figure 2D) and by laser ablation experiments in earlier work (Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 2D and by a citation to Blankenship et al., 2006.

claim: T1 events can be explained quantitatively through a simple geometric criterion that defines a 'T1 threshold' in terms of the local tension configuration and the local isogonal strain.
source: We have found that T1 events can be explained quantitatively through a simple geometric criterion that defines a 'T1 threshold' in terms of the local tension configuration and the local isogonal strain.
evidence: This claim is based on the geometric analysis presented in the study.

claim: A minimal mathematical model demonstrates how positive tension feedback can drive the tensions towards the T1 threshold and thus generate active T1s.
source: A minimal mathematical model of an intercalating cell quartet demonstrates how positive tension feedback can drive the tensions towards this T1 threshold and thus generate active T1s.
evidence: This claim is based on the minimal model presented in the study.

claim: Passive T1s result from external forces changing the isogonal modes until a cell neighbor exchange occurs, while tensions remain constant.
source: In contrast, passive T1s result from external forces changing the isogonal modes until a cell neighbor exchange occurs, while tensions (and thus interface angles) remain constant.
evidence: This claim is based on the minimal model and the analysis of passive T1s.

claim: The minimal model shows that no additional active mechanism is necessary for interface extension.
source: Our mathematical model for an intercalating cell quartet also sheds light on the long-standing puzzle of how interfaces extend after a neighbor exchange, even though cortical myosin can only exert contractile forces. We show that no additional active mechanism is necessary.
evidence: This claim is based on the minimal model.

claim: The minimal model captures interface extension as a purely passive process.
source: Our minimal model captures interface extension as a purely passive process.
evidence: This claim describes a key feature of the minimal model.

claim: In the minimal model, interface extension during both active and passive intercalations is driven by the tension on adjacent interfaces which exceeds the low active contractility of the new edge.
source: In our model, interface extension during both active and passive intercalations is driven by the tension on adjacent interfaces which exceeds the low active contractility of the new edge.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of interface extension in the minimal model.

claim: The low myosin level on the emerging interface is predicted by a simple model for the myosin 'handover' during a neighbor exchange.
source: The low myosin level on the emerging interface is predicted by a simple model for the myosin 'handover' during a neighbor exchange.
evidence: This claim describes the handover mechanism in the minimal model.

claim: In tissue-scale simulations, the model reproduces experimental observations that were previously taken as evidence for actively driven interface extension.
source: In tissue-scale simulations (Claussen et al., 2024), the model reproduces experimental observations (interface extension even if tissue extension is blocked, generation of irregular cell shapes) that were previously taken as evidence for actively driven interface extension (Collinet et al., 2015; Vanderleest et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by results from the companion paper and citations to Collinet et al., 2015 and Vanderleest et al., 2022.

claim: The findings on the dynamics of interface length and tension during active T1s are similar to another recently proposed model.
source: Our findings on the dynamics of interface length and tension during active T1s (Figure 2D) are similar to another recently proposed model (Sknepnek et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sknepnek et al., 2023.

claim: The model of Sknepnek et al., 2023 extends the classical 'vertex model' with area–perimeter elasticity by active cortical contractility.
source: This model extends the classical 'vertex model' with area–perimeter elasticity by active cortical contractility.
evidence: This claim describes the model of Sknepnek et al., 2023.

claim: Like in the minimal model presented in this study, active T1s in the model of Sknepnek et al., 2023 are driven by a positive feedback loop of cortical tension.
source: Like in our model, active T1s are driven by a positive feedback loop of cortical tension.
evidence: This claim compares the minimal model with the model of Sknepnek et al., 2023.

claim: The minimal model presented in this study requires fewer parameters than the model of Sknepnek et al., 2023.
source: Since our model is formulated in adiabatic force balance, it requires fewer parameters than the one of Sknepnek et al., 2023 and might be obtained from the latter in the limit of fast mechanical relaxation and dominant active tensions.
evidence: This claim compares the minimal model with the model of Sknepnek et al., 2023.

claim: In other recent theoretical work, Drosophila germ band extension has been interpreted as resulting from tissue fluidization.
source: In other recent theoretical work, Drosophila extension germ band has been interpreted as resulting from tissue fluidization (Wang et al., 2020), i.e., the loss of resistance to shear stress due to the vanishing of cortical tensions (Farhadifar et al., 2007; Yan and Bi, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020; Farhadifar et al., 2007; Yan and Bi, 2019.

claim: Laser ablation experiments show that cortical tensions remain finite during the morphogenetic process.
source: However, laser ablation experiments (Ma et al., 2009; Collinet et al., 2015) show that cortical tensions remain finite during the morphogenetic process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2009 and Collinet et al., 2015.

claim: Interfaces under vanishing tension would generically buckle into a wiggly shape.
source: In fact, interfaces under vanishing would generically buckle into a wiggly shape (as observed, for instance, in the amnioserosa during dorsal closure Tah et al., 2023 and in mutants with increased medial myosin Latorre et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tah et al., 2023 and Latorre et al., 2018.

claim: Wiggly interfaces are not observed in the Drosophila ectoderm during gastrulation where interfaces instead appear taught straight.
source: This is not observed in the Drosophila ectoderm during gastrulation where interfaces instead appear taught straight, serving as a simple visual indicator of finite tension.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the imaging data.

claim: Tissue mechanics was investigated in the regime where the tissue has internally generated tension at all times and hence is a solid rather than a fluid.
source: We have, therefore, investigated tissue mechanics in the regime where the tissue internally generated tension at all times and hence is a solid rather than a fluid.
evidence: This claim describes the regime in which the study was conducted.

claim: Tissue flow occurs as a result of internally driven plastic rearrangements, and does not require or imply tissue fluidization.
source: Tissue flow occurs as a result of internally driven plastic rearrangements, and does not require or imply tissue fluidization.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the study.

claim: The capacity of epithelial tissue to internally rearrange in a controlled manner may be thought of as active plasticity and falls beyond the fluidization paradigm.
source: The capacity of epithelial tissue to internally rearrange in a controlled manner – which may be thought of as active plasticity – falls beyond the fluidization paradigm.
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the findings.

claim: A striking alternating pattern of cortical tensions was found that explains how T1s are coordinated between neighboring cells.
source: We found a striking alternating pattern of cortical tensions that explains how T1s are coordinated between neighboring cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of local tension configurations.

claim: The prevalence of the alternating tension pattern is quantified by an order parameter for LTC.
source: The prevalence of this organizing motif is quantified by an order parameter for LTC.
evidence: This claim describes the LTC order parameter introduced in the study.

claim: LTC order precedes intercalations in lateral ectoderm.
source: LTC order precedes intercalations in lateral ectoderm and the loss of LTC order correlates with the slowdown of tissue flow at the end of GBE.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The loss of LTC order correlates with the slowdown of tissue flow at the end of GBE.
source: LTC order precedes intercalations in lateral ectoderm and the loss of LTC order correlates with the slowdown of tissue flow at the end of GBE.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: LTC order is driven by positive tension feedback and requires an initial regular hexagonal packing of cells.
source: We show that LTC order is driven by positive tension feedback and requires an initial regular hexagonal packing of cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from tissue-scale simulations presented in the companion paper.

claim: Intercalations disrupt the regular hexagonal packing and thus lead to the loss of LTC order as GBE progresses.
source: Intercalations disrupt this regular hexagonal packing and thus leads to the loss of LTC order as GBE progresses (see illustration in Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from tissue-scale simulations and is illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: Loss of LTC order and degradation of coherent tension orientation cause T1s to become incoherent and ineffective at driving tissue flow.
source: Together with the degradation of coherent tension orientation, loss of LTC order causes T1s to become incoherent and, therefore, ineffective at driving tissue flow.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from tissue-scale simulations.

claim: Convergent extension flow is self-limiting and the final tissue shape is encoded in the initial degree hexagonal order and tension anisotropy.
source: Taken together, this implies that convergent extension flow is self-limiting and that the final tissue shape is encoded in the initial degree hexagonal order and tension anisotropy.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from the study and tissue-scale simulations.

claim: Disrupting the hexagonal packing of nuclei prior to cellularization will prevent the emergence of LTC order and thus cause slower GBE.
source: Moreover, we predict that disrupting the hexagonal packing of nuclei prior to cellularization will prevent the emergence of LTC order and thus cause slower GBE.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings of the study.

claim: Convergent extension of the germ band must be compensated by an orthogonal deformation of the dorsal tissue, the amnioserosa, because the Drosophila embryo is a closed surface.
source: Because the Drosophila embryo is a closed surface, convergent extension of the germ band must be compensated by an orthogonal deformation of the dorsal tissue, the amnioserosa (see Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is based on geometric considerations and is illustrated in Figure 9A.

claim: To achieve the compensatory deformation, the mechanical properties of the tissue must be modulated along the dorsoventral axis.
source: To achieve that, the mechanical properties of the tissue must be modulated along the dorsoventral axis: Positive tension feedback drives active rearrangements in the lateral ectoderm, and tension homeostasis in the amnioserosa allowing it to yield to external forces while maintaining tissue integrity.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the study.

claim: The DV-axis patterning is important for achieving the compensatory deformation.
source: This highlights the importance of the DV-axis patterning.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the role of DV patterning.

claim: Recent work has shown that mechanical feedback loops in the embryo are patterned along the DV axis.
source: Recent work (Gustafson et al., 2022) has shown that mechanical feedback loops in the embryo are patterned along the DV axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2022.

claim: The DV patterning system is conserved across species.
source: Notably, the DV patterning system is conserved across species (Holley and Ferguson, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holley and Ferguson, 1997.

claim: Because the coherent T1s observed do not mix cells in the tissue, distinct DV fates remain clearly demarcated.
source: Our work also highlights a second interaction between tissue flow and DV patterning: because the coherent T1s we observe do not mix cells in the tissue (Figure 1A), distinct DV fates (e.g. neural and surface ectoderm) remain clearly demarcated, a clear biological necessity.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of coherent T1s and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In addition to the DV gradient, tension anisotropy along the DV axis is required to orient the GBE flow along the AP axis.
source: In addition to the DV gradient, tension anisotropy along the DV axis is required to orient the GBE flow along the AP axis.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of how tension anisotropy orients tissue flow.

claim: The tension anisotropy might be due to mechanics or due to AP-striped genetic patterning.
source: This anisotropy might be due to mechanics (pulling of the ventral furrow [Gustafson et al., 2022] and hoop stresses resulting from ellipsoidal embryo geometry [Lefebvre et al., 2023] since we observe anisotropy already prior to VF formation), or indeed due to AP-striped genetic patterning (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Lavalou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Thanks to the positive tension feedback, a weak initial anisotropy is sufficient to bias the direction of tissue elongation.
source: Thanks to the positive tension feedback, a weak initial anisotropy is sufficient to bias the direction of tissue elongation.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of how positive feedback amplifies initial anisotropy.

claim: Twist and snail mutants, which have significantly reduced initial myosin anisotropy, still extend their germ band, albeit at a slower rate.
source: This explains why twist and snail mutants, which have significantly reduced initial myosin anisotropy, still extend their germ band, albeit at a slower rate (Gustafson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2022.

claim: Genetic patterning and self-organization are interconnected during GBE.
source: Our findings show how genetic patterning and self-organization are interconnected during GBE.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Genetic patterning provides tissue scale input by demarcating distinct tissue regions with different mechanical properties.
source: Genetic patterning provides tissue scale input by demarcating distinct tissue regions with different mechanical properties.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the role of genetic patterning.

claim: Self-organization via positive tension feedback orchestrates myosin contractility on the cellular scale and drives T1s.
source: Self-organization via positive tension feedback orchestrates myosin contractility on the cellular scale and drives T1s.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the study.

claim: Mechanical self-organization via tension feedback allows cells to coordinate their behaviors on the tissue scale to give rise to coherent morphogenetic flow.
source: In the companion paper (Claussen et al., 2024), we show that mechanical self-organization via tension feedback also allows cells to coordinate their behaviors (such as active T1s) on the tissue scale to give rise to coherent morphogenetic flow.
evidence: This claim is supported by results from the companion paper.

claim: No genetic mechanism has been found that produces cell scale coordination from predetermined genetic patterns alone.
source: As of yet, no genetic mechanism has been found that produces cell scale coordination – as manifested, for instance, in the alternating pattern of high and low tensions (Figure 8A, center) – from predetermined genetic patterns alone.
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Many interfaces in the lateral ectoderm that undergo T1 transitions at late stages of GBE are initially oriented along the AP, rather than the DV axis and only rotate into DV alignment briefly before they collapse.
source: Moreover, many interfaces in the lateral ectoderm that undergo T1 transitions at late stages of GBE are initially oriented along the AP, rather than the DV axis and only rotate into DV alignment briefly before they collapse (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: An initially set-up genetic pattern is not sufficient to explain the coordination of cell rearrangements.
source: This shows that an initially set-up genetic pattern is not sufficient to explain the coordination of cell rearrangements, in line with evidence from tissue scale analysis (Lefebvre et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and by a citation to Lefebvre et al., 2023.

claim: The emerging overarching picture is that of morphogenesis driven by an interplay of bottom-up local self-organization controlled by top-down genetic patterning that sets initial conditions and modulates parameters on the tissue scale.
source: Instead, the emerging overarching picture is that of morphogenesis driven by an interplay of bottom-up local self-organization controlled by top-down genetic patterning that sets initial conditions and modulates parameters on the tissue scale (Schweisguth and Corson, 2019; Lenne et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schweisguth and Corson, 2019 and Lenne et al., 2021.

claim: This interplay has recently been shown to underlie posterior midgut invagination, where genetic patterning initiates and channels a wave that mechanically propagates due to a local feedback mechanism acting on myosin.
source: Indeed, this interplay has recently been shown to underlie posterior midgut invagination, where genetic patterning initiates and channels a wave that mechanically propagates due to a local feedback mechanism acting on myosin (Bailles et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bailles et al., 2019.

claim: Geometric insight into tension space is expected to provide a new perspective on many different systems.
source: Going forward, we expect that geometric insight into tension space will provide a new perspective on many different systems (Shindo, 2018), for example, Xenopus neural tube formation (Butler and Wallingford, 2018), amniote primitive streak formation (Voiculescu et al., 2007; Saadaoui et al., 2020; Rozbicki et al., 2015), wing disk elongation (Dye et al., 2021; Dye et al., 2017), the sea urchin archenteron (Hardin and Weliky, 2019), or kidney tubule elongation (Lienkamp et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It will be interesting to study intercalations driven by actin 'protrusions' as they too are governed by cortical force balance on the cellular level, making tension inference and the tension–isogonal decomposition applicable.
source: Furthermore, it will be interesting to study intercalations driven by actin 'protrusions' (Weng et al., 2022): they too are governed by cortical force balance on the cellular level, making tension inference and the tension–isogonal decomposition applicable.
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by a citation to Weng et al., 2022.
